subject: Climate & Environment
title: Green Roofs and Walls
description: A micro-lesson that makes Green Roofs and Walls usable.

hook.text: A green roof can reduce a building's cooling costs by 25%. It also absorbs rainwater like a sponge.

buildup.text: Plants on rooftops insulate in winter, cool in summer, and filter air pollution.

discovery.text: Green walls — vertical gardens on building facades — clean air and reduce noise in dense neighborhoods.

twist.text: Toronto requires green roofs on all new buildings over 2,000 square meters — a city-wide mandate.

climax.text: Singapore aims to be a city in a garden — with green covering every surface including skyscrapers.

punchline.text: When the ground runs out of space for nature, the buildings take over.

quiz.question: How much can a green roof reduce cooling costs?

details.summary: Green roofs and living walls cover building surfaces with vegetation that absorbs rainwater, insulates interiors, reduces urban heat, and supports biodiversity. They can lower rooftop temperatures by up to 40 degrees Celsius compared to conventional surfaces and extend roof membrane lifespan.
details.whyItMatters: As cities heat up and storm flooding increases, green roofs offer a nature-based solution that simultaneously cuts energy costs, manages stormwater, and improves urban air quality.
takeaways: Green roofs can reduce surface temperatures by up to 40 degrees C
They absorb rainwater and reduce urban flooding
Vegetation insulates buildings, cutting heating and cooling costs

faq.question: How much do green roofs cost compared to regular roofs?
faq.answer: Green roofs cost two to three times more to install than conventional roofs, but they last longer, reduce energy bills, manage stormwater, and can increase property values. Lifecycle cost analysis often shows them as competitive or cheaper over 30 to 50 years.

faq.question: Can any building support a green roof?
faq.answer: Most flat and low-slope roofs can be retrofitted with lightweight extensive green roofs using sedum or grasses. Intensive green roofs with deeper soil and larger plants require stronger structural support. Engineers assess load capacity before installation.
